title: Cap. VIII: Disertius opposition; παρακοῆς names actual sin
pass_a_gloss: Garissoles's next move: Paul could hardly have pointed more plainly or strongly to the imputation of Adam's sin than by these words, which set Adam's disobedience cleanly against Christ's obedience. Placeus's counter-question: why then did the leading expositors of the verse fail to find that imputation in Paul's wording, and even push it away? Garissoles continues the contrast: the text means Christ's historical act of obedience — Christ became obedient to the Father as far as the cross (Philippians 2:8) — and therefore also means Adam's historical act of breaking the command. Placeus then wonders how the learned opponent can refuse to let the Greek παρακοῆς name Adam's actual sin. The opponent adds a hedge: the word does not name actual sin peeled away from the corruption that actual sin bred in Adam. Placeus shrugs at the hedge. Key: Placeus's own published wording said παρακοῆς points to Adam's sin as such — not bare actual apart from habitual, but actual together with habitual. Does saying that amount to denying that the word names actual sin? Placeus thinks not.
pass_b_english: Next, he says, the Apostle could scarcely have marked the imputation of Adam's sin more clearly or forcefully than these words do, with their sharp opposition between Adam's disobedience and Christ's obedience. How then did the greatest men, expounding that verse, fail to notice that imputation in the Apostle's words — and rather reject it? But let him go on: it marks Christ's actual obedience, by which Christ became obedient to the Father unto the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8). Therefore it also marks Adam's actual disobedience, by which he violated God's command — so it is strange that the learned man denies that by the word παρακοῆς the Apostle designates Adam's actual sin. As for his addition that it does not designate actual sin cut off from the corruption that sin produced in Adam, I care little. To affirm, in Placeus's own words, that παρακοῆς signifies Adam's sin alone — not as actual cut off from habitual, but together with habitual — is that denying that the word designates Adam's actual sin?
source_text: Deinde, inquit, vix disertius & efficaciùs poterat Apostolus imputationem Adamici peccati significare, quam factum est his verbis, claram oppositionem continentibus inter Adami inobedientiam, & obedientiam Christi. Qui factum est igitur, ut maximi viri versum illum exponentes, imputationem illam in Apostoli verbis non animadverterint, sed rejecerint potius? verum pergat, Obedientiam Christi actualem significat, qua Christus factus est obediens Patri usque ad mortem crucis, Phil. 2.8. Ergo & obedientiam Adami actualem, qua Dei mandatum violavit: ut mirum sit qua ratione neget Vir doctus hic παρακοῆς voce ab Apostolo designari peccatum Adami actuale. Nam quod addit, non designari peccatum actuale praecisum à corruptione, quam in Adamo peperit, hoc parum moramur. Quid, affirmare voce παρακοῆς solum peccatum Adami significari, non quidem actuale praecisum ab habituali, sed simul cum habituali, quae sunt Placei verba, estne negare, ea voce designari peccatum Adami actuale?
